paper_title: TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agentic services alternate between model inference on clustered GPUs and external tools on distributed CPUs. In this scenario, existing systems (1) overlook tool-return readiness in service evaluation, wasting limited resources, and (2) use heuristic strategies to decide admission and placement on GPUs, resulting in suboptimal scheduling decisions. To bridge this gap, we present TAO, a tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. Its value interface combines near-term tool readiness, node-specific cache credit with time-aware decay, and token footprint; a dynamic program jointly selects and places waiting sessions under capacity constraints. Across the 12 reported model-workload-concurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the best evaluated state-of-the-art baseline for each metric.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances in language models have expanded their use beyond basic chatbots to complex agents, making CPU-based tool execution substantial source of latency alongside GPU-based inference (Qiao et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Specifically, an agent operates through an agent session that alternates between LLM inference and external tools, such as compilers and retrievers, to complete multi-step tasks (Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026). When tools run outside the inference service, sessions demand for GPU computation becomes interruptible. We call this serving scenario Clustered-GPUs with Distributed-CPUs (CGDC), illustrated in Figure 1(Left): clustered GPUs, i.e., nodes, provide shared inference capacity, while external tool calls introduce delays between LLM requests1. Hence, efficient agentic serving must account for both inference demand and tool timing to sustain throughput and session responsiveness. We find that existing serving systems generally follow an evaluate-then-decide scheduling pattern (Guy et al., 2025; SGLang Team, n.d.; vLLM Production Stack Team, n.d.). They evaluate node features at the session level and then decide where and when to serve each session. This separates the problem into two related challenges: (1) how to value sessions next model turn, and (2) how to select and place sessions under shared capacity constraints. For session evaluation, existing systems in CGDC scenarios generally overlook tool-call latency when evaluating established workload features. Cache-aware systems reuse KV prefixes and balance inference load (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025); workflow-aware systems anticipate future calls (Wadlom et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026); and latencyaware schedulers prioritize sessions using latency or remaining-work estimates (Choi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Tool timing provides another useful signal, yet timing is utilized only as surrogate for KV reuse or token count: Li et al. (2025) predicts tool duration to choose KV-cache retention times, while Kang et al. (2026) discounts the token footprint of sessions executing tools as time elapses. Such features commonly enter fixed scoring rules or manually chosen thresholds. Corresponding author. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: Left: In the CGDC serving scenario, external tool calls create intervals between LLM requests and opportunities to reallocate inference capacity. Right: Two scheduling challenges motivate TAO, including (1) overlooking tool-return readiness and using heuristic merging for evaluation, and (2) making myopic and suboptimal decisions about session admission and placement. For decision making, existing systems usually apply heuristic scheduling strategies to each session, leading to myopic and suboptimal placements. In llm-d and SGLang (Guy et al., 2025; SGLang Team, n.d.), per-session scoring and routing rules assign inference opportunities individually. Yet sessions compete for the same node capacity. In particular, assigning one session can prevent more valuable combination of other sessions from being served. Furthermore, the heuristic selection and placement rules can also lead to suboptimal choices (Peng et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). As shown in Figure 1(Right), they fail to formulate scheduling jointly across multiple sessions. To address these challenges, we propose TAO, Tool-Aware jOint scheduling framework for LLMbased agentic serving. To incorporate tool latency into session evaluation, we propose tool-return readiness and explicitly integrate it with established features such as KV-cache reuse. Following Kang et al. (2026), we interrupt sessions during tool calls and put them into waiting pool. Toolreturn readiness estimates which sessions will need inference within the next scheduling window. For each sessionnode pair, we form value triplet from readiness, time-decayed KV-cache reuse, and token footprint. Given these evaluation triplets, we design joint scheduling algorithm in the decision making stage that considers all sessions in the waiting pool. Across deployments in different scenarios, joint optimization considers how the admission of each session affects the placements available to others. The optimizer maximizes the additive evaluation triplets using dynamic programming. Their coordinates evolve with cache age and tool progress, allowing distinct signals to guide decisions over time without weighted sum. Separating the optimization procedure from session evaluation makes the framework extensible. We summarize our contributions as follows: We identify the Clustered GPUs with Distributed CPUs (CGDC) serving scenario in the era of LLM-based agents, which shifts the key bottleneck of latency to tool calls. We propose TAO, tool-aware joint scheduling framework for LLM-based agentic serving. It improves the evaluate-then-decide paradigm through session evaluation with explicit tool-return readiness and decision making with joint modeling and optimization. TAO can be generalized and extended to different workloads such as multi-agent orchestration and Looped Agents. Moreover, it is also compatible with non-agent chatbot scenarios. Across the 12 reported modelworkloadconcurrency settings, TAO reduces latency by up to 26.8%, reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by up to 36.3%, and increases decode throughput by up to 29.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baseline for each metric.

sections.title: 2 BACKGROUND AND PROBLEM DESCRIPTION
sections.content: 2.1 AGENT SESSION AND DISTRIBUTED RESOURCES An agent session is persistent interaction that alternates between model requests and external tool calls. During model request, it uses serving node; during tool execution, it awaits result outside the inference service. scheduler records each sessions state and controls session admission, while the serving engine manages physical KV-cache residency and eviction.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: A later model request can reuse the KV prefix produced by earlier turns and avoid prefill computation (Kwon et al., 2023). Because an agent session carries its instructions, history, and tool observations across turns, reuse depends on both the agent session history and the node selected for its next request. SGLang and Preble exploit related prefix structure in model programs and distributed scheduling (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025). Our CGDC separates clustered GPU inference from distributed tool execution. Client or remote tools introduce variable delays between model requests, while their CPU and RAM are managed outside the GPU admission budget (Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026; Chang et al., 2026). Tool latency therefore determines when an agent session may need GPU resources for inference again. 2.2 SESSION INTERRUPTION AND SESSION RESTART During tool execution, session can release its GPU resources safely, although its cached prefix may subsequently be evicted. In contrast, preempting an active inference session requires recomputation. Repeated recomputation and reconstruction cause KV-cache thrashing, wasting capacity on state that must be rebuilt. This phenomenon motivates cache-aware engine and scheduling work (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025), as well as policies that weigh retaining state against serving other work (Li et al., 2025; Abhyankar et al., 2024). Therefore, at tool boundary, the scheduler can apply session interruption. Specifically, scheduler can interrupt the agent sessions model admission and release its node resources while the external tool continues. When inference service is needed again, session restarting restores admission on an eligible node and resumes the existing interaction. Session interruption and session restarting describe session state transitions. They are decoupled from the underlying inference engine. We find that the decisions made for these two operations can be based on the same session evaluation. Thus, we optimize toward unified goal for maximizing the evaluation. Session interruption can be decided by ordering sessions according to their values. Interrupted sessions join new arrivals in waiting pool. We focus on unified session evaluation and restarting decisions from this pool.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: PagedAttention and RadixAttention improve engine-level KV management, while Preble, Mooncake, and Dynamo exploit distributed cache locality (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025). SMetric combines session affinity with load balancing (Wang et al., 2026a), and production schedulers support extensible scoring (Guy et al., 2025). Autellix prioritizes programs using service history, while ThunderAgent introduces the lifecycle and waiting pool on which TAO builds (Luo et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026). InferCept and Continuum manage KV retention across tool calls, with Continuum using historical tool-duration distributions (Abhyankar et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). TAO brings cache opportunity and tool readiness into joint schedulerlevel admission and placement objective, complementing engine-level KV management. Parrot and Helium exploit workflow dependencies, while KVFlow and CacheScout guide residency or prefetching using execution structure (Lin et al., 2024; Wadlom et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). TOPAS jointly considers prefix residency and admission through bounded search and greedy packing (Ni et al., 2026). Conveyor, Sutradhara, and PASTE reduce exposed tool latency through partial execution, overlap, or speculation (Xu et al., 2024; Biswas et al., 2026; Sui et al., 2026). TAO converts tool timing into near-term model-service opportunities that inform joint admission and placement. AgentSysBench and MARS motivate accounting for tool delays and deployment boundaries (Chang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). TAO couples an agentic value interface with joint placement and asynchronous revalidation, using the insights from classical multiple-knapsack and generalized-assignment machinery (Kellerer et al., 2004; Shmoys & Tardos, 1993). It becomes popular to formulate some optimization problems in LLM and agentic serving and solve online, from edge scenarios (Li et al., 2026) to large-scale infrastructure (Bu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026).

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Tool execution makes agentic inference demand intermittent, while accumulated context makes the choice of node consequential. TAO brings these two properties into common scheduling objective through cache credit, tool-return readiness, and token footprint. Joint dynamic-programming placement maximizes this objective under snapshot capacity constraints, and asynchronous revalidation connects the plan to live execution. Across the evaluated DeepSeek-V4 Flash and Qwen3-32B settings, this design delivers improvements of up to 26.8% in latency, 36.3% in mean TTFT, and 29.5% in decode throughput. The resulting architecture gives agentic serving an extensible way to translate workload knowledge into coordinated admission and placement. We did not use generative AI to run experiments, fabricate measurements, or decide which experimental artifacts are valid. We reviewed all AI-assisted text and figure suggestions against the source code, experiment records, cited literature, and the compiled manuscript. sections.title: E COMPATIBILITY
sections.content: E.1 FALLBACK COMPATIBILITY Table 5 evaluates five schedulers on single TP8 node across 464 workers. Each run serves the 300task SWE-Lite workload through MiniSWE. This experiment checks that TAO remains competitive when concurrency is low and scheduling has less opportunity to improve performance. At 48 workers, its mean task latency stays within 2.3% of the best baseline, it retains over 92% of the best baselines decode throughput, and its mean TTFT is only 1520 ms above the best baseline. Thus, TAO incurs little task-latency degradation at low concurrency while maintaining competitive throughput. Together with its leading performance in the main evaluation (Section 4.2), this fallback behavior supports choosing TAO as the default scheduler across the evaluated operating regimes. E.2 KV-CACHE MANAGEMENT COMPATIBILITY TokenCake uses workflow dependencies and agent priorities to guide its Space Scheduler, and toolstall events and timing prediction to guide offload and upload in its Time Scheduler (Bian et al., 2025). Agentix prioritizes and preempts LLM calls using program-level service history to reduce requestand program-level blocking (Luo et al., 2026). It operates at the request-scheduling layer, so integrating it with TAO would require coordinating the two admission policies. KVFlow represents workflow as an Agent Step Graph and uses steps-to-execution to prioritize cache eviction and prefetching (Pan et al., 2025). CacheScout learns execution transitions online to guide cache management without requiring predefined graph (Zhang et al., 2026). These mechanisms provide information about future cache use. In our formulation, such information can inform the programnode values supplied to session evaluation, while engine-local cache policies can operate beneath TAOs admission and placement decisions. This is an architectural extension for KVFlow and CacheScout, while the implemented composition evaluated here uses TokenCake. With TokenCake enabled, the combined system completes validated 300-task SWE-Lite runs on DeepSeek-V4 Flash TP42 at 16 and 32 workers. TAO builds on these locality and load-balancing principles with joint optimization of assignments for waiting agent sessions under shared capacity. This joint view accounts for how one admission consumes capacity needed by other sessionnode assignments. Program-level schedulers also preserve information across model calls. KVFlow uses an Agent Step Graph and steps-to-execution to guide eviction and prefetching (Pan et al., 2025); CacheScout learns execution transitions online without predefined graph (Zhang et al., 2026). Their predictions guide context residency and prefetching; readiness supplies binary near-term admission-opportunity signal derived from tool timing. SAGA combines workflow graphs, session-affinity batching, and work stealing (Guo et al., 2026). TOPAS also uses heuristic state searching: it scores prefix-residency and request-admission states using remaining workflow paths, movement costs, and downstream reuse, with bounded candidate search and greedy packing (Ni et al., 2026). Its task-dependent utility and engine-level residency decisions differ from our fixed additive value contract and exact multi-node scheduling problem. Prediction also supports latency-oriented scheduling. ELIS predicts response length, while Kairos combines workflow-aware priority with memory-aware dispatch (Choi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Recent work separates already-ready turns from their release, using meanCVaR objective and an adaptive budget for committed inference work (Feng et al., 2026). This addresses tail-aware release after dependencies complete; TAO additionally evaluates near-term return opportunities during external tool execution. Complementary mechanisms change the execution timeline itself: Conveyor exposes partial tool execution, Sutradhara overlaps tool work and prefill through orchestratorengine cooperation, and PASTE speculates on future tools while coordinating tool execution with returning model agent sessions (Xu et al., 2024; Biswas et al., 2026; Sui et al., 2026).
